disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Combined Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development across multiple settings (e.g., work, home, social). Symptoms must have been present since childhood, although adults may first come to clinical attention when environmental demands exceed their coping strategies, revealing long-standing but previously compensated difficulties. The course is typically chronic, with manifestations evolving over time—hyperactivity may become more subjective restlessness in adults, while organizational and planning difficulties often become more prominent. It is distinguished from mood, anxiety, and personality disorders by its early onset, cross-situational cognitive/behavioral pattern, and the absence of episodic mood changes or primary motivational or comprehension deficits.

narrative.personality: Keri is a routine-driven, detail-focused craftswoman who finds comfort in order, hands-on work, and quiet, home-centered hobbies.
narrative.stressor: Keri’s difficulties became more pronounced when she semi-retired from full-time fabrication and shifted into part-time consulting and mentoring at the workshop, where her role changed from largely solitary production work to supervising multiple apprentices, juggling custom orders, and sitting through longer planning and safety meetings. The new demands on planning, multitasking, and paperwork disrupted the predictable rhythm she had relied on for decades and exposed long-standing attentional and organizational vulnerabilities that had been masked by highly routinized, hands-on tasks. Over the next two years, she found herself increasingly frustrated by her inability to stay put through meetings, keep to schedules, and follow through on mentoring sessions without drifting back to the shop floor, which led to tension with younger colleagues and self-doubt about her competency. When her supervisor gently suggested she might step back from certain responsibilities after others complained about her frequent pacing and leaving mid-discussion, and her husband echoed concerns about her restlessness at church and during senior-center activities, she agreed to seek a psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t seem to sit still in meetings anymore—I’m always getting up and walking around when I’m supposed to stay put.”

narrative.personality: Janelle is an energetic, socially outgoing planner who enjoys keeping busy with work, fitness, and community events, often pushing herself with caffeine-fueled enthusiasm.
narrative.stressor: Janelle’s challenges intensified when she was promoted from a basic front-desk role to an administrative specialist position in the school district, which required her to manage complex workflows, coordinate multi-departmental meetings, and participate in lengthy committee sessions. The job amplified demands on her ability to wait through structured agendas, listen to others finish before speaking, and manage multiple stakeholders’ needs, all while her social enthusiasm pushed her to volunteer for additional projects and after-hours events. Over the next two years, her tendency to jump into conversations, struggle with orderly turn-taking in meetings, and overcommit to tasks began to create friction with supervisors and colleagues, who perceived her as overly eager and occasionally disruptive despite her strong work ethic. After a tense performance review that highlighted her difficulty staying in her lane during discussions and complaints from coworkers about her interrupting in group settings, she recognized that these patterns were affecting both her advancement and her social relationships and sought psychiatric help to understand what was going on.
narrative.chief_complaint: “At work and in meetings I just can’t seem to wait my turn—I jump in before other people are finished and it’s starting to cause problems.”

narrative.personality: Howard is a conscientious, data-minded worker who enjoys structured, solitary tasks and hobbies, balancing methodical routines with occasional social outings.
narrative.stressor: Howard’s difficulties came to a head when his company expanded and he was promoted to coordinate a larger team and manage a denser schedule of vehicle and equipment cleaning contracts, which required sustained focus on planning, documentation, and supervising others rather than simply doing the hands-on work himself. The increased cognitive load—tracking multiple jobs, safety checks, and eco-friendly chemical protocols—made it much harder for him to stay mentally engaged from start to finish on tasks that no longer provided the immediate, tangible feedback he enjoyed. Over the ensuing two years, he noticed growing frustration with his inability to maintain focus during longer jobs, safety briefings, and team meetings; this led to scheduling errors, missed procedural steps, and criticism from his manager, which undermined his confidence despite his efforts to compensate with apps and checklists. When a near-miss safety incident was traced back to his lapses in keeping track of the sequence of tasks, and his wife pointed out similar struggles following through on home projects and even sitting through book club discussions, he became worried about jeopardizing his job and finally agreed to a psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I just can’t seem to stay focused on a task at work long enough to see it through, even when I know it’s important.”
